content: Post-mortem: the flashed image booted to garbage because --gc-sections discarded .boot_magic — nothing referenced it, so link-time garbage collection threw the section away and the ROM check at 0x0800_01C0 read 0xFFFFFFFF. Fix: KEEP(*(.boot_magic)) in link.x plus a #[used] on the static. Verified by objdump -h before/after.
Decided: link with rust-lld, not GNU ld. Flags: -C link-arg=-Tlink.x -C link-arg=--nmagic. GNU ld padded load segments to 64K pages and blew the 16KiB budget.
UART DMA receive uses the idle-line interrupt with a 50ms software timeout as backstop. Below 20ms we truncated frames from slow USB-serial adapters; above 200ms the flasher UX felt dead.

Gotcha for whoever touches the IWDG next: it is configured in window mode. Feeding the watchdog too EARLY resets the chip, same as starving it. The reset we chased for two days was a refresh inside the first 30% of the window, not a hang.
Stack region is painted 0xAA55AA55 at reset; the panic handler scans for the high-water mark and prints it. Caught the manifest parser using 3.1KiB of stack before we ever shipped.
Adopted flip-link: it relocates the stack below .bss so a stack overflow faults immediately instead of silently corrupting statics. Add it as the linker wrapper in .cargo/config.toml.

Bug: after programming a flash page the CPU sometimes executed stale bytes. Root cause: instruction cache. You must invalidate the icache (and the flash prefetch buffer via the ACR bits) after any write to flash that the CPU may execute. Added cache_invalidate() to flash_write().
DFU transfer chunk size is 4KiB, aligned to the flash page size. 1KiB chunks quadrupled erase-verify round trips; 8KiB chunks overflowed the RAM staging area on the 96K parts.

Decided: CRC32 for boot image integrity, not SHA-256. Rationale: this check is corruption detection only, not tamper resistance — authenticity comes from the ed25519 signature. A software SHA-256 cost 6.2KiB of the 16KiB ROM budget; the hardware CRC unit costs zero. Rejected alternative recorded so nobody 'upgrades' it back.

A/B image slots at 0x0801_0000 and 0x0804_0000. Boot picks the slot with the higher generation counter whose CRC passes; a rollback counter in RTC backup register 3 prevents downgrade past a revoked generation.

Field failure analysis: units bricked during battery sag were writing SPI flash below 2.7V. Enabled the brown-out detector at level 3 (2.9V) so we halt before the flash's own minimum write voltage. Do not lower this threshold.
panic=abort everywhere; panic-persist stashes the panic message in a .noinit RAM region so the app can report the bootloader's last words after the next reset.

Logging is defmt over RTT, 1KiB up-buffer. When the host debugger is slow the buffer overwrites oldest frames (BlockIfFull would deadlock the flash state machine). Accept dropped frames; never switch this to blocking.

Post-mortem: manifest parse died with an allocation failure — the bump allocator's 8KiB heap was exhausted by serde-json-core's scratch space on manifests with >24 entries. Fix: cap manifest entries at 16 and parse the entry table in place. If the heap is ever exhausted again, the error LED pattern is three short blinks.

VTOR requires 512-byte alignment on this core. The application vector table lives at offset 0x8000; the bootloader writes VTOR and does a msr msp before the jump. Getting the alignment wrong faults on the first interrupt, not at the jump — very confusing to bisect.
Removed semihosting println from the debug build: each call traps into the debugger and made boot 40x slower, which masked the DMA race we were hunting. RTT only from now on.

Config gotcha: we hold D+ pull-up for 100ms after clock init before enumerating. Without the delay, certain Windows hosts fail enumeration on cold boot and the flasher can't find the device until replug.

Bug: firmware update wrote pages that verified wrong. Flash writes can only clear bits (1->0); we skipped the page erase when the staging CRC matched a previous attempt, so the second write ANDed over old data. Fix: always erase, no clever skip. Reads that come back as bitwise-AND of two images are the tell.

Image authenticity: ed25519 signature over (header || payload digest). Two verifying key slots in ROM; slot 2 is the rotation spare. Rotation procedure: ship an image signed by slot 1 that burns the new key into slot 2, then revoke slot 1 via the fuse bank. Never ship a build that trusts an empty slot.
A leftover bkpt (debug assertion macro) in the release build hardfaults when no debugger is attached. CI now greps the disassembly for bkpt outside the panic path.

Boot timing after the LTO changes: 38ms cold boot to app entry (12ms of that is CRC over 192KiB app), 12ms warm boot when the valid-image flag survives in backup RAM. Budget is 50ms; we have margin for the signature check (~9ms measured).

CI runs the boot logic under QEMU (mps2-an385 machine). Good for the state machine and manifest parsing; useless for flash timing, brown-out, and cache behavior — those need the hardware rig. Don't trust green CI for anything analog.

RTC drifted ~3s/day. Root cause: LSE crystal load capacitors were sized for 12.5pF but the board has 9pF pads. Firmware-side calibration (RTC smooth calibration register, -87ppm) brought drift under 0.3s/day until rev C boards.

Race post-mortem: DMA half-transfer interrupt and the UART idle-line interrupt could both claim the same region of the receive buffer when a frame straddled the halfway mark. Symptom: occasional duplicated 16-byte runs in the flasher payload. Fix: double-buffer DMA with ownership handoff in one place, the idle ISR only records the cut point.

The CRC32 lookup table is built by a const fn at compile time and lives in flash. Computing it at boot cost 1.1ms and 1KiB of RAM; the table costs 1KiB of flash instead. Flash is the cheaper budget here.

Tooling: probe-rs flashes our image 2.4x faster than openocd (1.9s vs 4.6s for 192KiB) and its defmt integration is native. openocd stays documented for the one contributor on the ST-Link v2 clone that probe-rs rejects.

Heisenbug post-mortem: memory.x declared 128K of RAM but the -RB part only has 96K. The linker happily placed .bss where no memory exists; everything worked until the heap crossed 96K under load. Symptom was corruption that moved with code size. The linker cannot save you from a wrong memory map — added a boot-time RAM probe that walks the claimed range.

NVIC priority grouping is 4.0 (no subpriorities). DMA > UART > USB > SysTick. SysTick must be lowest or its tick handler preempts the flash state machine mid-erase and the busy-wait deadline math goes wrong.

Size budget check-in: 13.2KiB of the 16KiB ROM budget used. opt-level="z", lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic=abort. Biggest remaining items: usb descriptors 1.8KiB, manifest parser 2.1KiB. The signature verifier will need ~1.5KiB — we fit, barely.

Host flasher protocol: every 4KiB chunk is ACKed; on NAK or 500ms silence the host retries the same chunk up to 3 times, then aborts the whole session. Chunk sequence numbers are u16 and wrap — the bootloader only checks 'expected or previous', nothing fancier.

Bug post-mortem: the manifest parser kimi wrote read the length fields big-endian; the manifest spec is little-endian everywhere. It happened to work on symmetric test values (0x0100 sized entries). Added a manifest magic that is endianness-asymmetric (0x4D5A4B31) so a byte-order bug fails on the first field.

Clock init order matters: raise the flash wait states BEFORE switching sysclk to the PLL, and only start the peripheral clocks after the PLL reports lock. Doing it backwards runs flash reads out of spec — the MCU won't fault, it just fetches garbage instructions at random.

TODO: enable RDP level 1 (readout protection) once the signing chain lands, and validate that a debugger attach in the field wipes SRAM as the datasheet claims. Do this on a sacrificial board first — RDP regression to level 0 mass-erases flash.

The HardFault handler dumps stacked PC/LR/xPSR plus SCB->CFSR/HFSR over UART in a fixed 9-line format. The decode cheat sheet lives in docs/hardfault.md; IMPRECISERR with a store address in the flash range almost always means a write to a locked page.

Measured: enabling fat LTO plus panic=abort shrank .text by 11% (14.9KiB -> 13.2KiB) and cut boot CRC time by 0.8ms from better inlining of the byte loop. Thin LTO got only 4%. Build time cost: +9s, irrelevant for this crate.

External SPI flash is probed by JEDEC ID: 0xEF4017 = W25Q64, 0xEF4018 = W25Q128. Rev B boards shipped with either part, so the staging area size and sector map come from the probe, never from a compile-time constant.

Session handshake: client sends nonce, server replies with HMAC-SHA256 over (nonce || session_key_id || timestamp). Replays are rejected by a sliding window keyed on nonce. The window started at 30 seconds; see the clock-skew incident for why it is 90 now.

Fixed: tiny control messages were arriving noticeably late. Nagle's algorithm was coalescing them behind unacked data; set_nodelay(true) on every session socket dropped control-message latency from tens of milliseconds to microseconds. We batch application-side instead, so Nagle buys us nothing.
Outbound connect timeout is 3s, then exponential backoff 1s/2s/4s/8s capped at 60s, with 20% jitter. Without jitter, a relay restart had every client reconnect in the same 100ms slot.

Subtle bug: tokio::select! drops the losing future, which cancels an in-flight read_exact and loses the bytes it had consumed from the socket. Any cancellation-unsafe read must be wrapped in its own task or use a cancel-safe framed reader. We hit this as rare protocol desync under load; the framed codec fixed it.

UDP payloads capped at 1200 bytes. Path MTU discovery is unreliable across the NATs we see (ICMP black holes), and 1200 clears IPv6 minimum MTU (1280) minus headers with margin. Fragmented UDP effectively never arrives on real networks.

Decided: postcard, not bincode, for the wire format. Median message: 41 bytes postcard vs 68 bincode (varint lengths win on our small structs). postcard is also no_std, which the embedded probe client needs. Rejected: bincode (size), serde_cbor (slower, larger), hand-rolled (maintenance).

Incident: the relay died overnight, exit code 137. dmesg on the host shows the OOM killer chose it after resident set hit 11GB. Cause: the broadcast fan-out used unbounded channels; one slow consumer made every queued message immortal. See the bounded-channel decision that came out of this.

Decided: every inter-task channel is a bounded mpsc (capacity 1024) and every producer handles the full case explicitly — drop-oldest for state deltas, await for control traffic. Unbounded queues just move the failure to wherever memory runs out; a producer that cannot slow down is a design bug, not a tuning problem.

Post-mortem: after the relay maintenance restart, 40k clients stampeded back within two seconds and kept the accept queue saturated long enough that health checks failed, which caused a second restart — a self-inflicted outage loop. Mitigations shipped: jittered backoff client-side, SYN backlog raised to 4096, and health check grace period of 30s after listener start.

Decided: rustls for all TLS, no OpenSSL anywhere in the tree. Reasons: no C dependency to cross-compile, memory-safe, and the cert verifier is pluggable which the pinning code needs. ring's build takes 20s but caches well.

TCP keepalive set to 30s (probes 3, interval 10s). Consumer NAT boxes drop idle mappings around 60s and the connection just goes silent — no RST, nothing. 30s keeps the mapping alive; anything chattier wastes radio on mobile clients.

Frame layout: varint length prefix, then a one-byte tag, then payload. Max frame 16MiB — reject larger at the length prefix, before allocating. The length check must happen before reserve(); the fuzzer found the allocation-before-validation ordering bug in week one.

Relay throughput benchmark (c6i.4xlarge, 64-byte messages): 1.2M msg/s on a single shard, 4.7M msg/s with 4 shards pinned to separate cores. Bottleneck at 4 shards is the fan-out lock in the subscription map — sharding that map is the next win.

Evaluated QUIC via quinn for the client link. Verdict: not now. Wins were real (no head-of-line blocking, connection migration on network change) but 0-RTT resumption interacts badly with our replay window design and the CPU cost was +18% at current message sizes. Re-evaluate when the mobile roaming complaints justify it.

Incident: after the relay pool was re-IPed, half the fleet kept connecting to the old addresses for hours. Our in-process resolver cached lookups forever. Fixed: cache honors DNS TTL with a 30s floor and a 15min ceiling, plus cache bust on connect failure. Stale DNS looks exactly like a network partition from the inside.

Accept path: one listener socket per worker via SO_REUSEPORT instead of a shared listener behind a lock. Kernel does the load balancing; accept latency p99 fell from 1.8ms to 90us under connect storms. Caveat: rebalancing on worker death needs the socket to be recreated, handled in the supervisor.

Post-mortem: clients with clocks 40-70s off (cheap Android, no NTP) were rejected by replay protection and retried forever, looking like an attack. Widened the replay window from 30s to 90s and added a server-time hint in the handshake reply so clients can offset. Alert now distinguishes 'stale timestamp' rejects from 'duplicate nonce' rejects.

State sync sends deltas against the last acked snapshot; a full snapshot goes out every 64 ticks or when the delta would exceed half the snapshot size. Clients that fall more than 128 ticks behind get a fresh snapshot and a session flag we can graph.
Simulation tick is 32Hz. We tried 64Hz: p99 tick budget went from 61% to 97% utilization on the big shard and jitter got visibly worse, not better. 32 it stays until the shard split lands.

UDP hole punching succeeds for 78% of client pairs (measured over 30 days). The rest fall back to relaying through the TURN-like path. Symmetric NATs on both ends are the unfixable case; don't spend more time there.

cargo-fuzz on the frame decoder found a panic: truncated header made split_to(len) assert when len exceeded the buffer. The fix validates the length prefix against remaining bytes before any split. Fuzzer corpus is checked in under fuzz/corpus; run it after any decoder change.

Round-trip metrics use an HDR histogram (1us..10s, 3 sig figs), snapshot every 10s. Current steady state: median 1.9ms, 99th percentile 8ms, worst-of-day around 120ms which correlates with the hourly snapshot compaction.

SIGTERM starts a 5s drain: stop accepting, flush per-session send queues, send GOAWAY-equivalent, then close. Sessions still open at the deadline are cut. Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds must stay above the drain timeout or the kubelet SIGKILLs mid-flush.

Tried io_uring (tokio-uring) on the relay hot path: +15% throughput on kernel 6.8, but it pins us to recent kernels, complicates the seccomp profile, and the buffer lifecycle rules fight our pooling. Decision: shelved; revisit when the fleet baseline reaches 6.x everywhere.

Snapshot compression: zstd level 3 with a 16KiB dictionary trained on captured production snapshots. 61% size reduction vs uncompressed, 2.1x better than gzip at equal CPU. Dictionary version is negotiated in the handshake; mismatched dictionaries fall back to dictionary-less zstd.

Config gotcha: binding [::]:9000 gives you dual-stack on Linux only if net.ipv6.bindv6only=0; on some distros and on the BSDs the default differs, and Windows needs IPV6_V6ONLY cleared explicitly on the socket. We now always set the socket option ourselves instead of trusting the OS default. Symptom when wrong: IPv4 clients get connection refused while IPv6 works.

Relay-to-relay links pin the peer certificate's SPKI digest (SHA-256, base64) from the deployment manifest, on top of normal chain validation. This closes the man-in-the-middle window during CA compromise or mis-issuance. Pin rotation: ship new pin alongside old for one release, then drop the old.

Post-mortem: a client retry after a timed-out publish caused the order to apply twice — the first attempt had actually succeeded, the ack was lost. Every mutating message now carries an idempotency key (client id, sequence number); the relay keeps a per-session dedup window of 256 entries. Retries without idempotency keys are how you corrupt state politely.

Frame buffers come from a pool of BytesMut (4KiB slabs, capacity 4096 slabs). Allocation pressure dropped ~30% and p99 send latency stopped spiking during snapshot bursts. Slabs that grow past 64KiB are not returned to the pool — let the big ones die.

Payload checksum is CRC32C using the hardware instruction (SSE4.2 / ARMv8 CRC extension), ~9GB/s per core; the software fallback table does ~800MB/s. Feature-detect at startup, never at compile time — the fleet is mixed.

Per-stream flow control: 256KiB window, WINDOW_UPDATE at half consumed. A stream that stays full for 30s is treated as abandoned and reset. Global connection window is 4MiB so one stream can't starve the rest.

TODO: mutual TLS between relays — server certs are pinned already but client auth on the relay mesh is still bearer tokens. Blocked on the deployment manifest gaining per-node key issuance. Do this before the mesh leaves the private VPC.

CI has a netem harness: a network namespace pair with tc netem 5% loss, 80ms +-20ms delay, 1% reorder. The protocol suite must pass under it. It caught the select!-cancellation desync and two ack-timing bugs that clean-network tests never would.

Version negotiation: first byte of the hello is the max version the sender speaks; the reply pins the session to min(client, server). Minimum supported is v3 — v2 had the unauthenticated resume hole and is refused outright with a distinct close code so old clients log something actionable.

Dev tooling: switched the workspace to the mold linker (via .cargo/config.toml, linux only). Incremental link of the relay binary went from 14s to 2s; full release link 41s to 9s. CI release builds stay on lld — mold's --icf=all interacted badly with the perf-map symbols caliper needs.

Bug I introduced, for the record: the peer-address parser assumed a 4-byte address and indexed sockaddr bytes directly, so the first IPv6 client crashed the demo with a segfault in the unsafe block. Rewrote using socket2's typed accessors; the unsafe block is gone entirely. Lesson: no raw sockaddr punning outside the one vetted module.

Send scheduling: two priority classes per session. Control frames (acks, pings, flow control) preempt bulk (snapshots, deltas); bulk is round-robined across streams. Without this, a big snapshot delayed acks enough to trigger spurious retransmits on lossy links.

Config gotcha: axum is pinned at 0.7 (matchit 0.7), so route path params must use the colon form — .route("/v1/rules/:rule_id", ...). The brace form {rule_id} compiles fine but matches only the literal string, so the route silently never fires. Switch to braces only when upgrading to axum 0.8+.

Decided: journal_mode=WAL with busy_timeout=5000 and synchronous=NORMAL. WAL lets readers proceed while one writer is active; NORMAL trades a sliver of durability (a power cut can lose the last transactions, never corrupt) for not fsyncing the WAL on every commit. For a memory store that is the right trade.

FTS5 query strings are never passed through raw: sanitize_fts_query splits on whitespace and wraps every token as an escaped quoted phrase. Bare user input like a stray double quote, NEAR, or a column filter is a syntax error or an injection vector otherwise.

Known defect, kept deliberately: the older /v1/memory* handlers answer 200 OK with an {"error":...} body instead of real status codes. Fixing it breaks existing callers, so it waits for a version bump. The rule routes (400/404 via ApiResult) are the pattern to copy for any new endpoint.

rule add upserts by (scope, rule_id): re-using an id revises the rule in place — created_at survives, updated_at moves. Two competing copies of a rule are worse than none; that is why there is no separate 'rule edit'.

rule retire tombstones (status='retired'), never deletes. The row stays searchable — the record that a policy once applied is itself worth keeping in a memory store. Re-adding the same id reinstates it. Retiring twice is idempotent; retiring an unknown id is exit 3 / HTTP 404, not silent success.

Rule text containing the substring 'engram:rules:' is rejected at write time — rendered into the managed block it would terminate its own sentinel region and eat everything after it. An opening sentinel with no closing one in a target file is treated as mangled and replaced wholesale.

Scope resolution cascade: --scope flag, then ENGRAM_SCOPE, then git working-tree basename, then cwd basename; the response reports which via scope_origin. Tests that assert on scope must set ENGRAM_SCOPE or they inherit the runner's checkout name.

Under MCP the scope cascade resolves against the server process's cwd, not the client's. A shared engram MCP server therefore needs an explicit scope argument on every call, or every project writes into the scope named after wherever the server happened to start.

idx_memories_rule is a partial unique index: UNIQUE(scope, rule_id) WHERE rule_id IS NOT NULL. It enforces one rule per id per scope without constraining ordinary messages, whose rule_id is NULL. SQLite treats NULLs as distinct in plain unique indexes, but the partial form documents intent and keeps the index small.

All timestamps are ISO 8601 UTC via jiff, never local time (Standard §14). created_at/updated_at carry nanosecond precision with a Z suffix. If a timestamp ever renders without Z, something regressed.

rmcp pinned at 0.16; the #[tool_router]/#[tool_handler] macro shape changed across 0.x releases, so check cargo doc -p rmcp before touching mcp.rs. The v0.1.0 fix made the initialize handshake tolerant of clients that skip the notifications/initialized message — Claude Code sends it, some other MCP clients don't, and we used to hang waiting.

remember and rule add read content from stdin when the positional argument is omitted — that is how you pipe multi-line content without shell quoting pain: git log -1 | engram remember --scope release-notes.

Exit codes: 0 success, 2 invalid argument, 3 not found (unknown rule id, missing scope), 4 database error, 5 I/O. Machine-mode errors go to stderr as a structured envelope with the same code. Scripts should branch on the exit code, not parse the message.

memories_fts is kept in sync by AFTER INSERT/DELETE/UPDATE triggers on memories — no application-side dual write. If FTS ever drifts (it did once during a botched manual import), rebuild with INSERT INTO memories_fts(memories_fts) VALUES('rebuild').

migrate() probes pragma_table_info before each ALTER TABLE because SQLite has no ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS. Opening a pre-rules database upgrades it in place; both added columns are nullable so every pre-existing row remains a valid plain message. No migration table, no version pragma — the schema is its own record.

recall fetches the newest N rows for the scope (ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT n) and then reverses them, so output reads oldest-first like a transcript. Callers that want newest-first should not re-sort strings — created_at is the sort key, ids are not ordered.

search ranks with FTS5's built-in bm25() and default column weights. TODO: once agent/scope become FTS columns, weight content above them. Note bm25() returns lower-is-better; the ORDER BY is ascending, which reads backwards if you expect scores.

Database path resolution: --db flag beats ENGRAM_DB beats the default ./engram.db relative to cwd. The relative default is a footgun under MCP — the server's cwd decides, so wire an absolute path in the client config.

Color handling: --no-color flag or NO_COLOR env (any value, including empty per the spec) disables ANSI. Machine mode never emits color regardless. FORCE_COLOR is deliberately not honored — agents kept setting it globally and corrupting JSON consumers.

Output mode detection: --json forces machine mode; otherwise stdout-not-a-TTY or any of AI_AGENT/AGENT/CI set triggers it. Human mode is only ever a TTY nicety. This means engram recall | head is already JSON — no flag needed in pipelines.

Posture decision: the HTTP surface binds 127.0.0.1:8420 with no auth. Threat model is 'other processes of the same user', not the network. Anything that would change that (0.0.0.0, tailscale exposure) must add bearer auth first — recorded so a future 'just bind it wider' patch trips over this note.

The rendered rules block is a pure function of the active rules: ordered by rule_id, no generation timestamp, byte-identical across runs. That is what makes rule sync report 'unchanged' without writing, and therefore safe to run from a git hook or a session-start hook. Do not add a timestamp to the block.

Core model: a rule row in SQLite never reaches an LLM's context by itself. rule sync rendering into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md — files the harnesses auto-load — is the delivery mechanism, not an export convenience. A rule that has not been synced is a policy nobody is following yet; that is why add/retire responses carry a next_step.

Decided: the semantic-search upgrade path is sqlite-vec as a loadable extension with static embeddings (model2vec-style distilled vectors, computed in-process, no LLM calls at query time). Hybrid retrieval = FTS5 BM25 + vector cosine fused by RRF. Rejected: external embedding APIs (breaks the offline posture), a sidecar vector DB (two stores to keep consistent).

Fusion plan: reciprocal rank fusion with k=60 (the constant from the original Cormack paper), score = sum over lists of 1/(k + rank). k=60 damps the head enough that one list can't dominate; tune only against the held-out bench set, never against dev queries.

Confusing-behavior post-mortem: a long-lived reader connection in the MCP server kept an open read snapshot, so recall from that process returned rows as of its last transaction while a fresh CLI process saw newer memories immediately. Not corruption — WAL snapshot isolation working as designed. Fix: the server now runs each read in a fresh transaction instead of holding one open.

Post-mortem: SQLITE_BUSY errors under concurrent CLI + MCP writes even with WAL. Two writers still serialize on the write lock, and the default 0ms busy handler gives up instantly. busy_timeout=5000 makes the second writer wait its turn instead of failing. If 5s ever proves too short, the answer is a write queue, not a bigger timeout.

TODO: consider FTS5 prefix indexes (prefix='2 3') if prefix queries land in the UX. Costs index size (~15-25% typically); currently nothing issues prefix queries so it stays off. Measure on the bench corpus before enabling.

engram schema prints the JSON Schema for the data model as {"Memory": ..., "Rule": ...} — one object, two definitions. Generated from the serde types, so it cannot drift from the wire format. Agents should read this instead of guessing field names.

engram describe emits the CLI Standard capability manifest: commands, flags, env vars, exit codes, output modes, as JSON. It is the machine-readable contract; docs are prose over it. New commands must appear there in the same change.

role defaults to "note" on every surface (CLI, MCP, HTTP). Alternatives: user, assistant, system, rule (rule is set internally by rule add — do not pass it to remember). The default was chosen so pipeline glue that doesn't care about roles writes something honest.

Gap vs Standard §3: remember has no --dry-run yet (the Standard wants one on every write command). rule sync has one and it is genuinely useful (shows the would-be block). When adding it to remember, dry-run must still run scope resolution and validation, just skip the INSERT.

POST /v1/rules/sync is the only HTTP route that writes outside the database. Sync targets derive from the server process's cwd — AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md there — never from caller input; the CLI's --file override is deliberately not exposed over HTTP, so there is no path traversal surface. Consequence of the no-auth posture: any local process can rewrite that one project's agent files, and only those.

Release profile per Standard §3: lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, strip=symbols. Binary went 6.8MB -> 4.9MB. panic=abort means no catch_unwind anywhere in the tree — the HTTP layer must convert errors, not catch panics.

Baseline numbers on a 100k-row synthetic corpus (t14s laptop, NVMe): FTS5 MATCH p50 0.4ms, p99 2.1ms; recall-by-scope p50 0.2ms; insert 0.9ms including FTS trigger. Plenty of headroom — do not add caching in front of SQLite without a measured reason.

Decided for the retrieval bench: corpus documents carry stable string keys (slugs); the eval runner maps keys to fresh UUIDs at ingest time and keeps the mapping in memory. Slugs never enter the store — ids stay opaque, and the bench files stay diffable.

ENGRAM_AGENT provides the default --agent for rule add (and only rule add — remember requires an explicit agent). Set it in each harness's env so rules record which model wrote them without every prompt having to remember the flag.

All hot-path SQL goes through prepare_cached — rusqlite's per-connection prepared-statement cache. Statement parse cost only shows up under MCP where one connection lives for the whole session; the cache made recall-heavy sessions ~18% faster. The cache is per-connection, so the fresh-transaction fix did not invalidate it.

Event transport is a lock-free SPSC ring buffer per thread (64K events). On overflow we drop oldest and increment a dropped-events counter that exporters surface — a tracer that blocks the traced thread is worse than a tracer that admits gaps.

Decided: rdtsc for span timestamps, calibrated against CLOCK_MONOTONIC at startup and re-checked every 10s — but only when CPUID reports invariant TSC; otherwise fall back to clock_gettime. Non-invariant TSC on old Xeons drifted between sockets and produced negative span durations.

Post-mortem: traces showed impossible parent links after long sessions. Span ids were 32-bit random; by the birthday bound you expect a collision around 77k spans and our busy services emit that in minutes. Moved to 64-bit ids. The UI symptom (spans adopting the wrong parent) looked like an instrumentation bug and burned a week.

caliper export --folded emits collapsed stacks compatible with inferno/flamegraph.pl. Stack frames are semicolon-joined leaf-last; counts are nanoseconds, not samples, so flamegraph widths are time-proportional even with adaptive sampling.

CPU profiler samples at 999Hz, not 1000Hz — a sampler in lockstep with 100Hz/1000Hz periodic work aliases and either always or never sees it. Prime-ish off-round frequencies dodge the resonance. Same reason perf defaults to 4000-ish and not 4096.

JIT'd and dynamically generated code shows up in profiles only if the runtime writes /tmp/perf-<pid>.map (symbol, start, length per line). We emit it for our codegen'd matchers; without it those frames display as anonymous executable mappings.

Decided: build services with force-frame-pointers=yes and unwind via frame pointers; DWARF unwinding in-process was 20x slower per sample and the .debug_frame parsing pulled in 2MB. Measured cost of keeping rbp: ~2% throughput. Rejected: ORC-style tables (no rust toolchain support), LBR (perf-only, depth 32 limit).

Support issue post-mortem: a user's flamegraphs were all raw hex addresses — their release profile had strip=symbols, so the resolver had nothing to map. Resolution order is now: .symtab, then .gnu_debuglink file, then debuginfod if CALIPER_DEBUGINFOD_URLS is set. Docs now say: keep .symtab (strip=debuginfo, not symbols); the symbol table costs ~200KB and pays for itself the first bad day.

OTLP exporter: gRPC, batches of 512 spans, 5s flush timeout, at-most-once (no persistent queue — this is a tracer, not a message bus). Endpoint from OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT to stay compatible with collector conventions.

Instrumentation overhead benchmark: 3ns per span enter/exit pair when the ring has space (two relaxed atomics and a TSC read), 41ns when crossing a cache line boundary in the ring, ~0 when the thread-local is disabled. Sampling-profiler overhead at 999Hz: 0.7% CPU on the busy relay.

Bug class we keep re-hitting: spans vanish across tokio::spawn because the task starts with a fresh context — the parent span is thread-local and the executor moved us. Every spawn in instrumented code must be .instrument(span.clone()) or use our spawn_traced wrapper. Clippy lint caliper::bare_spawn now flags it in CI.

Post-mortem: uprobes attached at the wrong offset after a toolchain bump — the target function got inlined into two call sites and the symbol we probed was the cold outlined copy. Functions meant as uprobe attach points now carry #[inline(never)] and a #[no_mangle] alias under the caliper_probes namespace.

Hardware counter mode reads LLC-load-misses and LLC-store-misses via perf_event_open groups, sampled per span. On the relay workload, cache misses per message is the metric that predicted the p99 regressions — instructions-per-cycle stayed flat while misses doubled.

perf_event_open sample collection uses a 512-page mmap ring per CPU (2MB). Smaller rings lost samples during syscall storms; the kernel reports lost records in PERF_RECORD_LOST, which we now graph instead of ignoring.

Weird-data post-mortem: span durations in one customer's containers quantized to 4ms steps. Their runtime mounted a coarse clocksource (kvm-clock in a misconfigured guest); CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE granularity leaked into everything. We now sanity-check clock resolution at startup and warn when it is above 1us.

TODO: off-CPU profiling — sample sched_switch/sched_wakeup so we can attribute blocked time (locks, IO, page faults) to spans, not just on-CPU time. The eBPF plumbing from the syscall tracer should be reusable. This is the most-requested missing feature from the ironway team.

Local trace storage is SQLite in WAL mode, one file per host, spans table partitioned by day via the trace_date column. Retention job deletes day-partitions older than 14 days and runs PRAGMA incremental_vacuum. Same engine choice as engram, deliberately — one set of operational habits.

Symbol resolution results go through an LRU cache of 10k entries keyed by (build_id, address). Cold resolution touches disk (ELF parse) at ~40us; cached is ~0.9us — 40x. Cache is invalidated per build_id, so redeploys never serve stale names. Without it, symbolizing a busy trace dominated export time.

Post-mortem: the sampling profiler froze a customer process solid. SIGPROF fired while the thread held the allocator lock; our handler called a logging path that allocated; instant self-deadlock. Signal handler code is now audited async-signal-safe: pre-allocated buffers, write() only, no malloc, no locks, no panic formatting. There is a CI test that samples a malloc-storm binary for an hour.

caliper export --chrome emits Chrome trace-event JSON (the catapult format) so traces open in chrome://tracing and Perfetto. Use complete events (ph=X) not begin/end pairs — half-open pairs from crashed processes render as infinite spans.

Multi-host trace merge does not trust wall clocks: each host's offset is estimated from RPC request/response timestamp pairs (NTP-style, minimum-RTT filtered), residual skew typically <200us. Wall-clock ordering of events across machines is a lie we refuse to render — the merge tool orders by estimated offsets and shows the uncertainty band.

Sampling policy: head-sample at 1% but keep-if-error — any span that records an error flips its whole trace to kept at export time (tail-based). Requires buffering the trace until root span end or 30s, whichever first. The interesting traces are precisely the ones head sampling throws away.

Bug: a span guard's Drop panicked while another panic was unwinding — that is an instant abort. The guard's Drop is now panic-free by construction (all fallible work moved to explicit end()); Drop only swaps a pointer and increments the ring cursor. Lesson generalized into the code review checklist: Drop impls in library code must not panic.

Export failure post-mortem: batches with huge span attributes hit tonic's default 4MB gRPC message cap and the whole batch bounced. Now: per-span attribute values truncated at 4KiB with a truncation marker, batch splitter targets 1MB encoded size, and oversize single spans are dropped with a counter rather than poisoning the batch.

The syscall-latency eBPF program got rejected by the verifier after we added path recording — unbounded loop over path components. Fix: fixed 8-iteration unroll with explicit bounds checks each step. General note: write eBPF like the verifier is a hostile reviewer with no imagination, because it is.

Span-name filtering with user regexes cost up to 30% of ingest CPU. Now: a literal-prefix prefilter (memchr-based) runs first and the regex only sees candidates; common filters like 'http.*' are literal-prefix in practice. Ingest overhead with typical filters is back under 3%.

Gotcha: the OS reuses thread ids, so a trace merge keyed on tid alone interleaves two different threads' spans into one lane. Lane identity is (tid, thread_start_ns) — the start timestamp comes from /proc scanning at attach or the clone event when tracing from birth.

Panic post-mortem: span names are truncated to 128 bytes, and name[..128] panicked with 'byte index 128 is not a char boundary' on a name with a multibyte char straddling the cut. Truncation now uses floor_char_boundary-style logic and appends an ellipsis marker. Any &str[..n] on external input is a latent panic.

Ingest pipeline benchmark: 2.1M spans/s single collector core (decode + dedup + partition write), 7.8M/s across 4 cores before the SQLite writer serializes us. The writer batches 4096 spans per transaction; smaller batches halved throughput.

Exporter retry policy: 3 attempts with 1s/2s/4s backoff on transport errors only — 4xx-equivalent (bad data) never retries, that batch is dropped and counted. More retries just turned collector outages into client memory bloat; the dropped-batch counter is the honest signal.

CALIPER_FILTER uses RUST_LOG-style directives (target=level, comma-separated) with one gotcha: bare 'debug' sets the global level but 'caliper=debug' scopes to the crate — people keep writing 'CALIPER_FILTER=caliper' expecting debug and getting the default. An invalid directive is a startup warning listing the parsed result, not a silent no-op.

Evaluated adding allocation profiling; compared against heaptrack on the relay. Verdict: don't build our own yet — heaptrack's intercept covers the need for offline analysis, and our in-process hook doubled allocation cost in the worst case. Revisit if we need allocation attribution per span rather than per callstack.

Build failure post-mortem: fetchFromGitHub failed with 'hash mismatch in fixed-output derivation ... got: sha256-...'. Upstream had moved the release tag to a new commit. Policy: pin rev to a full commit sha, never a tag or branch, in every fetcher. Tags are mutable pointers wearing an immutable costume.

All flake inputs declare inputs.<name>.inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs". Before dedup we evaluated three nixpkgs revisions; closure size dropped 1.4GB and eval time halved. Check flake.lock for duplicate nixpkgs nodes after adding any input.

Decided: fenix for rust toolchains, not oxalica's rust-overlay. We need the exact rust-toolchain.toml channel plus the thumbv7em target and rust-analyzer from the same channel; fenix's fromToolchainFile does that in one line. Rejected rustup-in-devshell: impure, and CI can't cache it.

CI pushes to the spacecraft cachix binary cache after every main build: nix build --json | jq -r '.[].outputs.out' | cachix push spacecraft. Contributors get watch-exec in the devshell. Without the cache, a cold contributor build is ~35min; with it, ~90s.

Post-mortem: a build that worked on one laptop failed everywhere else — it was run with --impure and picked up PKG_CONFIG_PATH from the host. Removed every --impure from docs and CI; builds are sandboxed, and anything the build needs must be an explicit input. If a build only works impure, the flake is lying about its dependencies.

Decided: crane over naersk for the Rust packaging. crane's cargoArtifacts pattern caches the dependency build as its own derivation, so a source-only change rebuilds in ~40s instead of ~6min. naersk's dependency vendoring fought our git-dependency on rmcp. Rejected: buildRustPackage (rebuilds the world every time).

nixpkgs is pinned to a revision with glibc 2.39 because the embedded vendor toolchain dynamically links against the host sysroot in tests and 2.40 changed a symbol version it trips on. Revisit the pin when the vendor updates; tracked in the flake.lock comment.

The devShell provides mold and clang and sets CARGO_TARGET_X86_64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_LINKER=clang with -fuse-ld=mold via RUSTFLAGS. Nix-provided mold avoids the 'works on my distro' linker drift between contributors. Darwin falls back to the default ld64 — mold is linux-only there.

The NixOS module runs engram serve as a systemd service with DynamicUser=true, StateDirectory=engram, and ProtectSystem=strict. The database lives in /var/lib/engram/engram.db via the state directory. Port stays 8420 on loopback; the module refuses to render a config with a non-loopback listen address.

A scheduled CI job runs nix flake update weekly and opens a PR with the lock diff. Update PRs run the full test matrix including the VM test. Auto-merge is off on purpose: the openssl incident (see the unstable-bump note) is why a human reads the diff.

aarch64-linux builds cross-compile from x86_64 using pkgsCross.aarch64-multiplatform, with boot.binfmt.emulatedSystems qemu fallback for the test phase only. Native aarch64 CI runners were 4x slower than cross + qemu-test for our crate sizes.

The release job hit the build farm's 2h max-build-timeout — fat LTO on the static binary plus a cold cache pushed the link past it. Split the derivation so dependencies build separately (cacheable) and raised that one job's timeout to 3h. The farm kills at the timeout with just 'build timed out'; check timestamps in the log to confirm it wasn't a hang.

Post-mortem: a routine nixpkgs-unstable bump broke the build — openssl 3.2 -> 3.3 changed a deprecation into an error inside a transitive C dependency's configure. We were only on openssl because of a default feature in a transitive crate; that was the push to go rustls-everywhere (see the vendored-openssl rejection note). Pinned nixpkgs until the migration landed.

The home-manager module ships shell integration: ENGRAM_DB and ENGRAM_SCOPE exported per-project via direnv hook, plus completions for engram under zsh and nushell. It deliberately does not set ENGRAM_AGENT — that belongs to each harness's own config, not the shell.

Secrets are sops-nix with age keys: each host's key derives from its ssh host key (ssh-to-age), secrets/secrets.yaml is encrypted to all host keys plus the two admin keys. Rotation = re-encrypt with updated .sops.yaml recipients and redeploy; no secret ever lands in the nix store unencrypted.

Overlay post-mortem: our package override used 'prev' where it needed 'final', so it captured the un-overridden dependency and two versions of the library ended up in the closure — symptom was a confusing type mismatch between identically-named types. Rule: reach through 'final' for anything another overlay might touch; use 'prev' only for the package you are directly overriding.

Import-from-derivation is banned in CI (--option allow-import-from-derivation false). An IFD snuck in via a generated Cargo.nix and eval time went from 4s to 3min while forcing builds during evaluation. If a tool wants IFD, generate the file and commit it instead.

Dev machines: nix-collect-garbage --delete-older-than 14d freed 41GB on the first run. keep-outputs = true and keep-derivations = true in nix.conf so devshell roots survive GC — otherwise every gc re-downloads the toolchain the next morning.

The system flake registry pins nixpkgs to our lock's revision (nix.registry.nixpkgs.flake = inputs.nixpkgs), so ad-hoc 'nix run nixpkgs#foo' uses the same revision as the builds instead of hitting the network for whatever unstable is today. Makes scratch commands reproducible and mostly offline.

use flake . in .envrc with nix-direnv; nix_direnv_watch_file on rust-toolchain.toml and flake.lock so the shell reloads when either changes. Plain direnv without nix-direnv re-evaluates the whole flake on every prompt — that was the mysterious 3s shell latency someone reported.

The release artifact for engram is a fully static musl build: pkgsMusl + target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, RUSTFLAGS target-feature=+crt-static. Binary is 4.1MB, runs on any distro and in FROM scratch containers. Known cost: musl's allocator is slower under thread churn — irrelevant for a CLI, do not copy this blindly for the relay.

Config gotcha: every Cargo.lock change requires updating cargoHash in the package derivation. Workflow: set cargoHash = lib.fakeHash, build, copy the 'got:' hash from the mismatch error, paste. Forgetting it fails the build with a hash mismatch that names vendor-staging — that name in an error means stale cargoHash, not upstream tampering.

The flake ships a NixOS VM test: boots a machine with the engram module, waits for the systemd unit, then curls http://127.0.0.1:8420/health and asserts on a remember/recall round trip. It caught the StateDirectory permission bug that unit tests never could. Run it with nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.engram-vm.

aarch64 release builds go to a remote builder over ssh (nix.buildMachines): the builder connection uses its own dedicated ssh key with a from= restriction, not an admin key. Gotcha: the builder's nix daemon must trust our user for --builders to accept substitutes, or every build re-uploads the closure.

Weirdness post-mortem: nix kept evaluating a flake state that no longer existed — stale error about an attribute we had deleted. The flake eval cache (~/.cache/nix/eval-cache-v*) had a corrupt entry after a hard reboot. rm -rf of that directory fixed it. If nix seems to see a ghost of your flake, suspect the eval cache before your sanity.

allowUnfree = false globally; the only carve-out is an explicit allowUnfreePredicate for the vendor's flash tool, reviewed and documented. A silent allowUnfree = true would let unfree sneak into the closure unnoticed — the predicate makes each exception a diff someone approved.

TODO: publish the flake to FlakeHub once the VM test is green on both arches, and add the semver-tagged release workflow. Blocked on deciding whether the umbrella gets one flake or per-project flakes — leaning per-project with a meta-flake that composes them.

The embedded devshell composes gcc-arm-embedded (for the vendor's C SDK bits), the fenix toolchain with thumbv7em-none-eabihf, probe-rs, and flip-link. One nix develop .#embedded gives a bit-identical toolchain on every machine — the days of 'which arm-gcc do you have' are over.

nix-direnv registers gc roots for the devshell automatically under .direnv/. Side effect: those roots pin old toolchains after upgrades and disk fills quietly — .direnv can hold gigabytes across old shell generations. Periodically: find ~/code -name .direnv -maxdepth 3 | xargs du -sh, prune the stale ones.

Build farm post-mortem: with cores=0 and max-jobs=auto, two fat-LTO link steps ran concurrently and the 32GB builder started swapping until the kernel's memory killer took out the nix daemon. Settings now: max-jobs=2 with cores=16 on the builders, and the LTO derivations declare big-parallel so the scheduler spreads them. Link steps are memory-bound, not core-bound.

Substituters order: our cachix first, cache.nixos.org second. Gotcha that bit us: extra-substituters in a user's nix.conf silently does nothing for untrusted users unless the key is also in trusted-public-keys system-wide — the build 'works' but compiles from source for 35 minutes. The NixOS module sets both; non-NixOS contributors get a doc snippet to paste.

macOS: the nix sandbox is weaker and one test that resolved a relative path via /tmp symlinks (/tmp is /private/tmp there) failed only on darwin. The test now canonicalizes with realpath before comparing. CI matrix includes aarch64-darwin precisely to catch this class early.

The build embeds its provenance: version = "0.1.0-${self.shortRev or "dirty"}" flows into the crate via an env var the build.rs reads. A binary that can't tell you which commit built it is a support ticket with extra steps. 'dirty' in a released artifact fails the release check.

Decided: the vendored-openssl cargo feature is rejected umbrella-wide. It bundles a pinned OpenSSL that nix can't see, so CVE scanners miss it and the closure lies. Anything needing TLS uses rustls (ironway already standardized on it); if a dependency demands openssl-sys, we override it to link nixpkgs' openssl or we drop the dependency.

Key exchange preference order: sntrup761x25519-sha512 (when both sides support it), then curve25519-sha256. diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 is kept only as a last-resort server-compat option behind a config flag, and group14-sha1 is refused outright. The handshake logs the negotiated kex at debug level — first thing to check on 'connection reset during handshake' reports.

connect_timeout config key defaults to 10s (DNS + TCP + ssh banner exchange, together). The banner phase gets its own 5s sub-timeout because a firewall that accepts TCP then blackholes is the common failure and it should not eat the whole budget.

known_hosts parsing supports hashed entries (|1|salt|hash), @cert-authority, and @revoked lines. Gotcha: a HashKnownHosts entry can't be grepped for a hostname — the UI's 'which line matched' feature computes the HMAC per line instead. Port-nonstandard hosts hash as [host]:port.

Decided: agent forwarding is off by default and requires per-host opt-in. A compromised server with your forwarded agent can authenticate as you anywhere while the session lives. The error message when a remote tries names the config key rather than silently failing. Rejected: on-by-default with confirmation prompts (prompt fatigue makes them worthless).

Liveness defaults: ServerAliveInterval 15, ServerAliveCountMax 3 — a dead connection is detected within ~45s and the client exits with a distinct message instead of hanging forever. These are application-level (in the encrypted channel), so they also keep stateful middleboxes from expiring the flow.

Multiplexing post-mortem: control sockets failed with 'path too long' for users with deep home directories — unix socket paths cap at ~104-108 bytes and our default put the socket under the per-project config dir. Default moved to $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/anvil/%C where %C is a short digest of host-port-user. The mux test matrix now includes a 90-character home directory.

anvil keygen generates ed25519 only; RSA generation is behind --legacy-rsa (4096 minimum, and it prints a deprecation note). Verification still accepts rsa-sha2-256/512 signatures for old servers, but nothing anvil creates should start a new RSA lineage in 2026.

Interrupted transfers resume: the sftp backend records (offset, rolling checksum of last 64KiB) every 8MiB; on resume it re-reads the tail block from the remote, verifies the digest matches the local record, and continues from the offset — a silent remote-side change forces a full restart rather than a corrupt splice.

Bug: each -L local forward that failed its remote connect leaked the accepted local socket; a flapping backend piled up thousands of CLOSE_WAIT sockets until fd exhaustion. The accept path now wraps the socket in a drop guard tied to the channel-open outcome. lsof showing CLOSE_WAIT growth on the forward port was the diagnostic tell.

Slow-login investigation: users reported multi-second stalls before the password prompt on certain servers. Packet capture showed the delay server-side between banner and auth — classic reverse-DNS timeout on the sshd host. Client-side we now surface per-phase timings under -vv (dns/tcp/banner/kex/auth) so 'ssh is slow' reports arrive with the guilty phase named. Server fix remains UseDNS no.

The scp wire protocol is not implemented at all — anvil cp speaks sftp underneath while keeping scp-style UX. The scp protocol's filename handling is a command-injection minefield (remote filenames are shell-interpreted) and upstream openssh moved scp onto sftp too.

UpdateHostKeys-equivalent is on by default: after auth, the server's additional host keys are recorded so a future key rotation doesn't strand users on 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED'. Keys learned this way are marked in known_hosts comments with learned-at metadata for audit.

ProxyJump chains: -J bastion1,bastion2 nests transport channels; each hop authenticates independently and hostkey checking applies per hop (no blind trust of inner hosts because the bastion is trusted). Known limit: agent prompts for 3+ hop chains arrive in confusing order — the fix (serializing auth per hop) is on the board.

Post-mortem: a panic mid-session left the user's terminal in raw mode — no echo, no line editing, invisible typing. The raw-mode guard now restores termios via a scopeguard that runs on panic and on SIGTERM, and a panic hook re-runs it belt-and-suspenders. 'My terminal is broken after it crashed' should be extinct; stty sane is the user-side recovery if it ever recurs.

Windows terminal support uses ConPTY (min Windows 10 1809); the winpty fallback was dropped — it garbled cursor-addressing sequences under TUI apps. Resize events flow VT-native. Known issue: ConPTY swallows the final frame of output on abrupt disconnects; buffered and flushed on close as a workaround.

anvil connect --retry reconnects with 1s/2s/4s.. backoff capped at 30s, full jitter, forever by default (it is an interactive tool; giving up is the user's call via ctrl-c). Auth failures never retry — only transport errors do, so a typo'd password can't lock an account through automation.

Compression defaults off. Benchmark: on LAN and fast links, zlib compression *reduced* sftp throughput (cpu-bound at ~180MB/s compressed vs 980MB/s raw) and added latency jitter to interactive sessions. It helps only on genuinely slow links; the flag exists, the default respects the common case.

Rejected: a FIPS-validated crypto module build. It would freeze us onto a validated-but-stale primitive set (no sntrup761 hybrid), the validation cost is absurd for a personal-posture project, and Anvil-SSH's general-use posture promises quality, not certification. Revisit only if a real deployment contractually requires it.

keyboard-interactive auth is fully supported for one-time codes and multi-prompt flows: prompts render exactly as the server sends them (no caching, no auto-answer), echo flag honored per prompt. TOTP-style second factors work; what does not exist is any attempt to remember or replay a one-time answer.

Channel window tuning: default window 2MiB with 32KiB max packet (up from openssh-ish 64KiB defaults). On a 100ms-RTT high-bandwidth path, sftp throughput went 11MB/s -> 47MB/s — the window, not the cipher, was the bottleneck. Interactive channels keep a small window so a runaway cat doesn't buffer megabytes ahead of ctrl-c.

Key-file permission checks now open first, then verify via fstat on the open fd — the original check-path-then-open sequence was a check-then-use race, and the error message named the wrong path when a symlink was involved. User-visible behavior unchanged (group/world-readable private keys are refused with the chmod 600 hint); the internals just stopped being racy.

Interactive sessions set TCP_NODELAY — a keystroke is a tiny write and Nagle would batch it behind the previous echo's ack; that is visible typing latency on >40ms RTT links. Bulk sftp channels leave Nagle alone: throughput path, coalescing is fine there.

Auth events emit structured JSONL (one object per line: ts, host, user, method, outcome, kex, fingerprint) to the audit log when audit_log is configured. Line-oriented so it tails and greps; schema documented in docs/audit.md and versioned with a schema field. Nothing secret is logged — no key material, no passwords, ever.

Reminder for all agents: Anvil-SSH is the umbrella's only general-use posture project. That means semver discipline, a CHANGELOG.md entry for every user-visible change, and a deprecation cycle (one minor version minimum) before removing any config key or flag. Personal-posture shortcuts that fly elsewhere do not fly here.

cargo-audit runs in CI on every PR plus a nightly schedule. RUSTSEC-2024-0344-class advisories in transitive deps: policy is upgrade if a fix exists, otherwise document the exposure assessment inline in deny.toml with an expiry date — no permanent silent ignores.

SendEnv forwards LANG and LC_* by default (matching openssh custom); AcceptEnv on the server side decides. Gotcha we document: a server without the client's locale generates 'setlocale: No such file or directory' noise — anvil detects the reply and hints at the cause instead of letting users blame the terminal.

Throughput benchmark, localhost loopback, 1GiB transfer: sftp get 980MB/s with aes128-gcm@openssh.com, 610MB/s with chacha20-poly1305 (no AES-NI advantage), 47MB/s over the simulated 100ms link pre-window-tuning. Cipher ranking flips on machines without AES-NI; chacha20 is the portable default, aes128-gcm negotiated when hardware supports it.

Security-adjacent bug: bracketed-paste escape sequences pasted into the password prompt were stored as part of the password (and echoed garbage on some terminals). The prompt now strips bracketed-paste framing and rejects control characters in password input outright. Found via a user who 'could ssh from every terminal except one'.

TODO: FIDO2 resident-key support (sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com) — hardware-backed keys are the right default story for laptops. Needs the usb-hid stack decision first (hidapi vs ctap2 crate). Park webauthn-style attestation; nobody audits attestations anyway.

Release tarballs are static musl builds cross-compiled with zig cc as the linker driver (cargo-zigbuild): one build host produces x86_64 and aarch64 artifacts, glibc-version-independent. The nix flake does the same for the nix-native path; zig covers the plain-tarball path. cargo-zigbuild's target must include the .2.17 glibc suffix trick only for the glibc builds — musl needs no suffix.

fork no longer eagerly duplicates the address space: parent and child share pages marked read-only, and the page-fault handler copies a page only on first write (copy-on-write). fork+exec of a large process went from 40ms to 1.1ms. The refcount lives in the page frame struct; the last writer un-shares in place.

Decided: 4ms scheduler quantum (250Hz tick effectively) after measuring: 1ms quantum cost 3.8% throughput to context-switch overhead in the pipe benchmark, 16ms made the interactive shell visibly janky under load. Per-CPU runqueues, quantum refreshed on wake, no fancy vruntime yet.

TLB shootdown batches: unmapping N pages sends one IPI with a page list (up to 32 entries) instead of one IPI per page; above 32 pages we flush the whole TLB — the crossover measured at about 33 pages on our test boxes. munmap-heavy workloads stopped spending 20% of time in IPI handling.

Kernel object allocation is slab-based: per-CPU magazine caches over central slabs, objects constructed once and reused. kmalloc for odd sizes rounds to the nearest slab class; allocation fast path is lockless off the per-CPU magazine. Slab poisoning (0x5A pattern) is on in debug builds and caught two use-after-free bugs in the vfs layer.

Boot regression post-mortem: the kernel stopped being multiboot2-bootable — the linker script section shuffle moved the multiboot2 header past the first 32KiB of the image, where the spec says loaders stop searching. The header section is now first via explicit placement plus KEEP, with an assertion in the linker script: ASSERT(multiboot_header_end - image_start < 32K).

Deadlock post-mortem: CPU took a spinlock, an interrupt arrived on the same CPU, the IRQ handler tried the same lock — classic self-deadlock, machine frozen with no panic. Any lock that can be taken from interrupt context must be acquired with interrupts disabled (spin_lock_irqsave). Added a lockdep-lite debug mode that records which locks are ever taken in IRQ context and screams on a mismatch.

Timekeeping decision: TSC-deadline mode for the scheduler timer where CPUID advertises it (one MSR write to arm, no IO), HPET as calibration reference and fallback. The legacy PIT is used exactly once at boot to calibrate TSC frequency when the CPUID leaf doesn't report it.

earlyprintk goes to the 16550 UART at 0x3F8 with polled writes — works from the first instruction after protected-mode entry, before paging and before interrupts. Everything until the MMU is up logs there; the framebuffer console attaches much later. QEMU flag: -serial stdio. When the kernel dies silently before serial init, it died in the first ~200 instructions; use QEMU's -d int,cpu_reset.

Kernel stacks are 16KiB with an unmapped guard page below; overflow faults immediately instead of corrupting the adjacent allocation. The double-fault handler runs on its own IST stack so a stack-overflow-induced fault can actually be reported — without IST it would triple-fault and reboot with no output.

Context switch microbenchmark (pipe ping-pong, same core): 800ns per switch after the lazy-FPU change, down from 1.4us — saving/restoring SIMD state only when the task actually used it since last switch is most of the win. Cross-core adds ~2.1us from the IPI and cache effects.

virtio-net driver: descriptor rings sized 256, checksum offload negotiated via VIRTIO_NET_F_CSUM, and the receive buffer strategy is pre-posted 2KiB buffers with the mergeable-rxbuf feature for large frames. Gotcha: forgetting the available-ring memory barrier before the notify write cost a day — the device saw stale descriptor indices and randomly dropped transmits.

Post-mortem: a rust userland binary faulted at entry — its PT_LOAD had p_align 2MiB (huge-page linker default) and our loader assumed p_vaddr % PAGE_SIZE == p_offset % PAGE_SIZE at 4KiB only. The loader now honors segment alignment properly and maps with the file-offset congruence rule instead of assuming; the ELF spec is precise here and we were sloppy.

Syscall ABI: numbers are append-only and never reused (a deleted syscall's slot returns ENOSYS forever); arguments in rdi/rsi/rdx/r10/r8/r9 following the linux custom so ported code's expectations hold. TODO: vDSO for clock_gettime — currently every timestamp is a full syscall and the tracing folks feel it.

SMP bring-up: APs start in 16-bit real mode at a fixed sub-1MiB trampoline page (copied there at boot, 4KiB-aligned as SIPI requires); the trampoline switches to long mode with a minimal identity map, then jumps to the per-CPU entry with its stack pointer handed over via a mailbox word. INIT-SIPI-SIPI with the canonical 10ms/200us delays — shortcuts here work in QEMU and fail on hardware.

FFI discipline: every boundary crossing assembly or C stubs is extern "C" with #[no_mangle], and unwinding across it is undefined behavior — kernel Rust is built panic=abort so a panic can never unwind into asm frames. The three remaining C files (early boot shims) compile with -fno-omit-frame-pointer to keep the unwinder's view coherent.

The idle loop executes hlt with interrupts enabled (sti;hlt pair — the one-instruction interrupt shadow matters, sti then separately hlt has a lost-wakeup race). Busy-spinning idle cooked laptops and skewed every benchmark that shared the machine. mwait evaluation is a TODO gated on power measurement rig time.

PS/2 keyboard driver: IRQ1, scancode set 2 with the 0xE0 extended prefix state machine, translation off (we program the 8042 ourselves and disable its set-1 translation). Gotcha: you must drain the 8042 output buffer before enabling the interrupt or the pending byte from POST wedges some controllers into silence.

Scalability fix: per-CPU runqueue structs were adjacent in a static array and their lock words shared a cache line — every lock op on one CPU invalidated the line for its neighbor (false sharing). #[repr(align(64))] on the runqueue struct bought 18% on the 8-core scheduler stress test. Audit rule: any per-CPU struct with an atomic in it gets cache-line alignment.

Debug workflow: qemu -s -S, then gdb target remote :1234 with the kernel ELF for symbols; hardware breakpoints (hbreak) before the MMU flips on, regular breakpoints after. The .gdbinit in the repo loads the pretty-printers for page-table entries. For triple-fault loops, qemu -d int shows the exception cascade — read it bottom-up.

copy_from_user/copy_to_user never trust userland pointers: the access is done through exception-table-annotated instructions, so a faulting user address returns EFAULT from the copy instead of oopsing the kernel. The range check against the user/kernel split happens first — the exception table handles 'unmapped', the range check handles 'hostile'.

wait_event_timeout: sleeping tasks park on a wait queue with a timer; wake condition is re-checked under the queue lock after every wakeup because wakeups are advisory (spurious wakeups exist by design — cheaper than exact-once delivery). Timeout resolution is the 4ms tick; callers needing finer sleep get the hrtimer path instead.

initrd is cpio newc format (same as linux): ASCII hex headers, 4-byte alignment, TRAILER!!! terminator. The parser is ~120 lines of no-alloc Rust and fuzzed. Gotcha: file data alignment is on the header+name, not from file start — the off-by-alignment bug made every file's first bytes garbage until compared against a reference extractor.
